title: Making 10 and doubles

summary.text: Ten beans are on the table, and a cup hides some of them. You can see 7. Can you know how many are hiding without lifting the cup? You will spill beans, hide beans and look in a mirror to find every pair of numbers that makes 10, and the doubles from 1 and 1 up to 5 and 5. You will also find out why people everywhere practise making ten, and not eight or twelve.
summary.art: A girl at a kitchen table looking at seven rajma beans beside an upturned steel tumbler, with her mother's hand resting on the tumbler.

intro.hook: There are 10 beans. You can see 7. How many are hiding under the cup?
intro.text: 3 beans are hiding. 7 and 3 make 10. You did not need to lift the cup, because you know the whole is 10 and you can see one part. Two numbers that join to make 10 are called a bond of 10. In this lesson you will find all of them yourself, with beans. You will also meet the doubles, such as 4 and 4.
intro.art: Seven beans in a row on a table next to an upturned steel tumbler, with a small question mark drawn on the tumbler.

chart.title: 10 beans in all. Some are under a cup.

outcomes: I can find all the pairs of numbers that make 10.
I can say the missing part of 10 when I know the other part.
I can show that 3 and 7 make the same number as 7 and 3.
I can say the doubles from 1 and 1 up to 5 and 5.
I can show a bond of 10 on a ten-frame and on my fingers.
I can say why people group things in tens, and that other numbers can be split in the same way.

terms.example: There are 10 beans on the table. The whole is 10.
terms.art: Ten beans inside one big chalk loop labelled 'whole: 10'.

terms.meaning: Some of the whole, but not all of it.
terms.example: 6 of the 10 beans are on the left side. 6 is one part. The 4 on the right side are the other part.
terms.art: Ten beans split by a pencil line into a group of six and a group of four, each labelled 'part'.

terms.meaning: Two parts that join to make a whole.
terms.example: 7 and 3 make 10. So 7 and 3 are a bond of 10.
terms.art: A circle with 10 in it joined by two lines to smaller circles holding 7 and 3.

terms.meaning: To find the number that joins with another number to give exactly 10.
terms.example: You have 8 laddus. 2 more make ten.
terms.art: Eight laddus on a plate and two more being added, with the numeral 10.

terms.meaning: To put parts together and find the whole. We write it with the sign +.
terms.example: 4 idlis and 6 idlis are put on one plate. 4 + 6 = 10.
terms.art: Two small plates of idlis being tipped onto one big plate, with 4 + 6 = 10 written above.

terms.meaning: The same amount. We write it with the sign =.
terms.example: 7 + 3 = 10 means that 7 and 3 together are the same amount as 10.
terms.art: A balance with seven and three beans in one pan and ten beans in the other, level.

terms.meaning: A number added to the same number.
terms.art: Four beans in front of a mirror and four more beans seen in the mirror.

terms.meaning: A box with two rows of five spaces. When every space is full, it holds exactly ten.
terms.example: You put 6 beans on a ten-frame. 4 spaces are empty. So 6 and 4 make 10.
terms.art: A ten-frame with six beans and four empty spaces.

terms.meaning: The same two parts added in the other order. The whole does not change.
terms.art: Three red beans and seven white beans in a row, and the same row seen from the other side of the table.

explanations.context: This card gives the names for what you saw in Spill the Beans: the whole, the parts and the number bond.
explanations.definition: A whole can be split into two parts. The two parts together always make the whole again. Two parts that make a whole are called a number bond.
explanations.description: Here is a worked example. There are 10 beans on the paper. The whole is 10. A line splits them: 7 on the left and 3 on the right. 7 is one part and 3 is the other part. Push them together and count. It is 10 again. We say '7 and 3 make 10'. We write 7 + 3 = 10. The sign + means 'and', or 'add'. The sign = means 'is the same amount as'. No bean was added and no bean was taken away. That is why the two parts must make 10 every time. Now you try it. Put 10 spoons in two groups and say the bond.
examples: 10 idlis: 6 on your plate and 4 on mine. 6 and 4 make 10.
10 fingers: 5 on one hand and 5 on the other. 5 and 5 make 10.
10 chappals at the door: 8 big ones and 2 small ones. 8 and 2 make 10.
explanations.art: Ten beans on paper split by a pencil line into seven and three, with '7 + 3 = 10' written underneath.

explanations.context: In Spill the Beans you moved one bean at a time across the line and wrote every way to split 10. This card sets the ways out in order.
explanations.definition: There are 11 ways to split 10 beans between a left side and a right side. They are the bonds of 10.
explanations.description: Start with all 10 beans on the left. Move one bean across. Now the left has 9 and the right has 1. Move one more: 8 and 2. Each time, the left side goes down by one and the right side goes up by one. The whole stays 10, because a bean that leaves one side lands on the other side. Going in order like this, you cannot miss a way. The ways are: 10 and 0, 9 and 1, 8 and 2, 7 and 3, 6 and 4, 5 and 5, 4 and 6, 3 and 7, 2 and 8, 1 and 9, 0 and 10.
examples: If one part is 9, the other part must be 1.
If one part is 4, the other part must be 6.
5 and 5 is in the middle of the list. It is the only bond where both parts are the same.
explanations.art: A staircase of eleven rows of ten beans, each row split one place further along, from 10 and 0 down to 0 and 10.

explanations.concept: Turn-around facts: 3 and 7 is the same as 7 and 3
explanations.context: In Spill the Beans, 3 and 7 came up, and so did 7 and 3. This card shows why they give the same whole.
explanations.definition: When you add two numbers, the order does not change the answer. 3 + 7 and 7 + 3 are both 10.
explanations.description: Here is a worked example. Put 3 red beans and 7 white beans in one row. Count them from the red end: 3 and then 7 more is 10. Now walk round the table and count from the white end: 7 and then 3 more is 10. They are the same beans, so the whole is the same. This is useful. If you know 7 + 3 = 10, you already know 3 + 7 = 10. So the 11 ways to make 10 are really only 6 different pairs. People call 3 + 7 and 7 + 3 turn-around facts.
examples: The 6 pairs are: 0 and 10, 1 and 9, 2 and 8, 3 and 7, 4 and 6, 5 and 5.
explanations.art: A row of three red beans and seven white beans on a table, with one child at each end counting towards the middle.

chart.title: Count red first, or white first

explanations.concept: The ten-frame shows the missing part
explanations.context: In Hide and Tell you had to say how many beans were hidden. This card shows a picture that makes the missing part easy to see.
explanations.definition: A ten-frame is a box with two rows of five spaces. The beans show one part of 10. The empty spaces show the other part.
explanations.description: Here is a worked example. Put 6 beans on a ten-frame. Fill the top row first. The top row holds 5, and 1 bean goes in the bottom row. Now look at the empty spaces. There are 4. So 6 and 4 make 10. You did not count from 1. You looked at the gaps. Your hands are a ten-frame too. Hold up 6 fingers. The 4 fingers that are folded down are the missing part. This also tells you about taking away. If 10 beans are there and you take away 6, the 4 are left. Taking away comes in a later unit.
examples: 8 beans on the ten-frame leave 2 empty spaces. 8 and 2 make 10.
A full top row and an empty bottom row is 5 and 5.
An egg box for 10 eggs with 7 eggs in it has 3 empty cups.
explanations.art: A ten-frame with six beans, five in the top row and one in the bottom row, and the four empty spaces lightly shaded.

explanations.context: In Mirror Doubles you put beans in front of a mirror and counted the beans and their mirror picture together. This card says what you found.
explanations.definition: A double is a number added to the same number. Double 3 is 3 + 3.
explanations.description: Here is a worked example. Put 4 beans in a row. Put 4 more in a row under them, one under each. Count them all: 8. So double 4 is 8. We write 4 + 4 = 8. The doubles up to 5 are: 1 + 1 = 2, 2 + 2 = 4, 3 + 3 = 6, 4 + 4 = 8, 5 + 5 = 10. Look at the answers: 2, 4, 6, 8, 10. They are the numbers you say when you count in twos. That is because a double is made of pairs: each bean in the top row has a partner in the bottom row. Many bodies are built as doubles. You have 5 fingers on one hand and 5 on the other. A butterfly has the same pattern on the left wings and on the right wings.
examples: Two idli plates with 3 idlis each hold 3 + 3 = 6 idlis.
Both hands held up are 5 + 5 = 10 fingers.
A domino tile with 2 dots on each half shows double 2.
explanations.art: Two rows of four beans, one row exactly under the other, with '4 + 4 = 8' written beside them.

explanations.context: In Spill the Beans, all 10 beans may land on one side and none on the other. This card asks whether that is a bond of 10.
explanations.definition: Zero means none. 10 and 0 make 10. Adding zero to a number leaves the number the same.
explanations.description: Suppose all 10 beans land on the left. The right side has no beans. We say the right side has zero, and we write 0. The two parts are 10 and 0, and together they still make 10. So 10 + 0 = 10 is a bond of 10 too. This rule was first written down in India. In the year 628, the mathematician Brahmagupta wrote a book called the Brahmasphutasiddhanta. He lived in Bhinmal, in what is now Rajasthan. His book gives rules for working with zero as a number. One rule says that a number added to zero is the same number.
examples: 10 laddus in the box and 0 on the plate: 10 + 0 = 10.
0 + 10 = 10 is its turn-around fact.
7 + 0 = 7. Adding nothing changes nothing.
explanations.art: A sheet of paper with a line down the middle, ten beans on the left and an empty right side labelled 0.

explanations.concept: Why do we practise making ten?
explanations.context: This card asks why this lesson is about ten, and not about eight or twelve.
explanations.description: Count your fingers. You have ten. Most people on Earth group things in tens, and the most likely reason is our ten fingers. We also write numbers in tens: 13 means one ten and three more. That is why making ten is so useful to us. But ten is our choice. Other people chose other groups. The Yuki people of California counted in eights. They counted the four gaps between the fingers of each hand. The Maya of Central America counted in twenties. In India and other parts of Asia, many people count on the joints of their fingers with the thumb. Each finger has three joints, so one hand counts to twelve. The beans do not care. Eight beans split into pairs of parts just as ten beans do. People do not all agree on how much of this is chosen.
examples: The bonds of 8 are 8 and 0, 7 and 1, 6 and 2, 5 and 3, 4 and 4, and their turn-arounds.
A dozen bananas is a group of twelve. An egg tray of 30 is three groups of ten.
If people had eight fingers, children would probably practise making eight.

perspectives.who: The view that ten is chosen
perspectives.explanation: People picked ten as their group because of their fingers. Which bonds we practise, and how we write numbers, are habits that people made and share.
Only the group and the names are chosen. The facts are not. Seven things and three things make ten things for everyone, whether they count in tens, eights or twenties.

explanations.art: Three hands side by side: one with ten fingers numbered, one with the four gaps between fingers marked, and one with a thumb touching the twelve finger joints.

explanations.concept: Other living beings add and take away too
explanations.context: This card is about chicks and honeybees who kept track of 'more' and 'fewer', and what scientists really found.
explanations.description: Humans are not the only animals who can work out a hidden amount. In 2009 Rosa Rugani and her team in Italy tested chicks who were three or four days old. Each chick had grown up with five small yellow balls and liked to stay near them. A chick watched 4 balls go behind one screen and 1 ball go behind another. Then she watched 2 balls move from the first screen to the second. Now the screens hid 2 and 3. She could not see any ball. About three times out of four, she walked to the screen that now hid 3. In 2019 Scarlett Howard and her team in Australia trained 14 honeybees. A bee saw some blue shapes or some yellow shapes. Blue meant 'fly to the picture with one more'. Yellow meant 'fly to the picture with one fewer'. The bees chose correctly about 7 times out of 10. Scientists argue about whether to call this adding.
examples: A chick sees 4 balls hidden, then 2 of them carried away. She acts as if she knows 2 are left there.
A bee who sees 2 blue shapes flies to the picture with 3 shapes.
Both tests used small numbers, up to 5. Nobody has shown a chick or a bee making ten.

perspectives.who: Scientists who say it is adding
perspectives.explanation: The chick had to keep track of balls she could not see, as some were added and some were taken away. That is what adding and taking away are.
The chicks and bees were right most of the time, not every time, and only with small numbers. They may be judging 'more' and 'less' in their own way, without exact numbers.

explanations.art: A small yellow chick facing two upright screens, with two yellow balls being moved on a thread from behind one screen to behind the other.

chart.title: What the chick saw go in, before 2 balls moved

explanations.concept: Stretch: doubles past ten, and making ten to add
explanations.context: This card goes further than Class 1. It is for a child who finds the bonds of 10 and the doubles to 5 easy.
explanations.definition: You can use a fact you know to find a fact you do not know yet.
explanations.description: Here are two worked examples. First, double 6. You know double 5 is 10. Six is one more than five. So double 6 is 10 and two more, which is 12. Second, 8 + 5. Put 8 beans on a ten-frame. Two spaces are empty. Take 2 of the 5 beans to fill them. That makes ten. 3 beans are left over. Ten and 3 more is 13. So 8 + 5 = 13. You used the bond 8 and 2 to get there. This is why knowing the bonds of 10 by heart helps with every bigger sum.
examples: Double 7 is double 5 and double 2: 10 and 4, which is 14.
9 + 4: 9 and 1 make ten, and 3 are left. 13.
7 + 5: 7 and 3 make ten, and 2 are left. 12.
explanations.art: A full ten-frame with eight dark beans and two light beans, and three more light beans beside it, labelled '8 + 5 = 13'.

agreed.text: If you split 10 things into two groups, the two groups always make 10 again.
agreed.evidence: Anyone can test it. Spill 10 beans on a paper with a line, as many times as you like. Count both sides. As long as no bean is lost or added, the two sides make 10.

agreed.text: You can add two numbers in either order and get the same answer.
agreed.evidence: Count a row of 3 red beans and 7 white beans from one end, then from the other end. They are the same beans, so both counts give 10.

agreed.text: Saying a sum again and again helps most after a child has seen why the sum is true.
agreed.evidence: In 1935 William Brownell and C. B. Chazal asked children how they got each answer, after weeks of drill. They concluded that drill works only when teaching that makes sense comes first.

agreed.text: Some other animals can keep track of small amounts being added and taken away.
agreed.evidence: Chicks a few days old chose the screen hiding more balls after balls were moved (Rugani and others, 2009). Trained honeybees chose 'one more' or 'one fewer' (Howard and others, 2019).

challenging.claim: Ten is a special number in nature.
challenging.context: This card is about whether ten is special by itself, or special only to people.
challenging.for: We have ten fingers. We write every number in tens. Money, measures and marks in school are counted in tens.
challenging.against: All of those are things people set up. Ten beans split into parts no differently from eight or twelve beans. Some peoples have counted in eights, twelves and twenties.

challenging.claim: Children should learn sums by saying them again and again, before they understand them.
challenging.who: Edward Thorndike, an American scientist, in 1922, and many schools since
challenging.context: This card is about an old argument: should number facts be drilled first, or understood first?
challenging.for: Practice does make answers quicker. A child who knows 7 and 3 make 10 at once has more attention left for harder sums.
challenging.against: William Brownell and C. B. Chazal found in 1935 that a quick right answer can come from a child who is still counting. They concluded that drill helps only after the child has seen why the fact is true.

challenging.claim: The sums are not chosen by anybody. 7 and 3 made 10 before there were people.
challenging.context: This card is about what is chosen in maths and what is not.
challenging.for: Everyone who splits ten beans gets the same bonds, in every country and every language. Nobody can vote to make 7 and 4 equal 10.
challenging.against: People chose to count beans as ones, to group in tens, and to call this amount 'ten'. Without those choices there is no sum to write.

big_questions.q: You cannot see the beans under the cup. How can you be sure how many there are?
big_questions.hint: What do you know about the whole? What could make you wrong?

big_questions.q: Why is 5 and 5 the only bond of 10 with two parts the same?
big_questions.hint: Try to make 10 from 4 and 4, or from 6 and 6.

big_questions.q: Can every number be split into two parts that are the same? Try 7 beans.
big_questions.hint: Put the beans in two rows. Does each bean have a partner?

big_questions.q: If people had eight fingers, would 7 and 3 still make 10?
big_questions.hint: Would the beans change? Would the names and the way of writing change?

big_questions.q: When you break a laddu into two parts, is anything lost?
big_questions.hint: Think about the crumbs. Think about the ten beans.

big_questions.q: A chick goes to the screen that hides more balls. Does she know a number, or does she feel 'more'?
big_questions.hint: She has no number words. How do you know 3 is more than 2?

story.title: The Boat That Went in Circles
story.note: Ammu, Unni, Meenu and the race are made up. In the boat races of Kerala the paddlers do sit in two rows, and a boat with more paddles pulling on one side does turn towards the other side. Real race boats also have people steering at the back. This small boat has nobody steering.
text: The old boat belonged to nobody, so it belonged to the children. It was long and narrow and dark with oil. It had five planks across it. Two children sat on each plank, one with a paddle on the left and one with a paddle on the right. Five planks. Ten paddlers.
Ammu was seven, and too small for a paddle. Her job was to sit at the very back with a coconut shell and scoop out the water that came in.
Her cousin Unni was eleven. He stood at the front and shouted the beat. 'Thi-thi-thara! Pull!'

On the morning before Onam, the children of the east bank raced the children of the west bank. They raced from the ferry jetty to the big rain tree. They did it every year. The east bank had lost every year that Ammu could remember.
'This year we have ten strong paddlers,' Unni said. 'Ten! Nobody is missing. I counted.'
The west bank boat was already on the water. Someone banged a steel plate with a spoon, and that was the start.
The children jumped in wherever there was room. They pulled. The boat shot forward. And then, slowly, the front of the boat began to swing to the right, towards the reeds.
'Straight!' shouted Unni. 'Go straight!'
The boat did not go straight. It curved like a banana. The children on the right dug their paddles in to turn it back. They lost three strokes. Then it happened again.
'Right side, you are lazy!' Unni shouted. 'Pull harder!'
The right side pulled harder. Their faces went red. The boat still swung towards the reeds. Far ahead, the west bank children were laughing.
Ammu stopped scooping. From the back of the boat she could see everyone's back at once. She looked along the left side, and then along the right side.
The left side looked long. The right side looked short.
She counted the left. One, two, three, four, five, six. Shanu and little Kunju were squeezed together on one plank, both paddling on the left.
She counted the right. One, two, three, four. There was a gap on the last plank, just in front of her.
'Unni chetta!' she called. 'We are six and four!'
'We are ten!' he shouted back. 'I counted! Ten is ten!'
'Six and four is ten,' said Ammu. 'Five and five is ten too. But six paddles push harder than four. That is why we keep turning.'
For a moment nobody pulled. The boat drifted.
'So we need one more paddler on the right,' said Unni. 'We do not have one more. We are only ten.'
'We do not need one more,' said Ammu. 'Meenu, come across.'
Meenu sat on the left side of the last plank, next to the gap. She lifted her paddle over her head and slid across. One fewer on the left. One more on the right.
Ammu counted again, out loud this time, so that everyone could hear. 'Left: five. Right: five.'
'Still ten,' said Meenu, sounding surprised.
'Pull!' shouted Unni.
They pulled. The boat went forward like a thread through a needle. Nobody had to turn it back. Every stroke took them towards the rain tree. The reeds slid by. The laughing ahead of them stopped.
They did not win. The west bank boat touched the rain tree's roots first, by the length of one paddle. But the year before, it had been the length of ten boats.
Unni sat down on the front plank. He was quiet for a while. 'I counted ten,' he said. 'Ten was right.'
'Ten was right,' said Ammu. 'But there are many tens. We had the wrong one.'
'Next year,' said Unni, 'you count us in. Both sides.'
Ammu picked up her coconut shell. There was a lot of water to scoop.
story.epiphany: For the parent: the same ten can be made in different ways, and the ways are not all alike. 6 and 4 is ten, and 5 and 5 is ten. Moving one child across takes one from the left and gives one to the right, so the whole stays ten. That is the same pattern the child finds in Spill the Beans. Only 5 and 5 is a double, with both sides the same.
ask: Unni counted ten paddlers, and he was right. So why did the boat keep turning?
Meenu moved from the left side to the right side. What happened to the number on each side? What happened to the whole?
Which other ways could ten children sit on two sides of a boat?
Why did the boat go straight only with five and five?

The boat curving towards tall reeds while a boy at the front shouts and the children on the right side strain at their paddles.
Seen from the back of the boat: six children's backs along the left side and four along the right, with a gap on the last plank.

experiments.title: Spill the Beans: how many ways can 10 be split?
experiments.context: In this test you spill 10 beans onto a paper with a line down the middle, again and again. Each time you count the left side and the right side. Then you hunt for every way that 10 can be split in two. You will find a pattern that tells you when you have found them all.
experiments.question: When 10 beans are split into two groups, which pairs of numbers can come up? How many different ways are there?
experiments.predict: Before the first spill, guess: how many beans will land on the left and how many on the right? Will it be the same every time? Why do you think so?
experiments.fair_test: We use the same 10 beans every time. We check that no bean has rolled away before we count. A bean that lands on the line is pushed to the side it is nearer to.

materials.item: dried beans such as rajma or chana, or tamarind seeds or buttons
a steel tumbler or cup, to shake and spill the beans
a sheet of paper with a line drawn down the middle
a towel or a tray to put the paper on, so that beans do not bounce away
a second sheet of paper and a pencil, for the tables

experiments.safety: Keep beans, coins and buttons away from babies and toddlers, who could choke on them.

schedule.what: Spill 10 beans six times and write down the two sides. Then move one bean at a time to find every way to split 10.

experiments.record: A grown-up draws two tables. The first has a row for each spill. The second has a row for each way found by moving one bean at a time. At the end the child says what they found, and the grown-up writes it under the tables.

example_chart.title: What a spill table can look like (your numbers will be your own)

setup.art: A sheet of paper with a pencil line down the middle lying on a folded towel, with a steel tumbler holding ten rajma beans beside it.
setup.caption: 1. Draw a line down the paper. Put 10 beans in the tumbler.

setup.art: A child's hand tipping the tumbler low over the paper, beans scattering on both sides of the line.
setup.caption: 2. Spill the beans from low down. Count each side.

setup.art: Ten beans all on the left of the line, and a finger sliding one bean across to the right.
setup.caption: 3. Later, start with all 10 on the left. Slide one bean across at a time.

flow.do: 1. Put the paper on a towel or in a tray. 2. Your child counts 10 beans into the tumbler. 3. Ask for a guess and a reason before the first spill. 4. Write the guess down.
flow.say: We will spill these 10 beans on the paper. How many will land on each side? Will it be the same every time? Why do you think so?
flow.kid: Count 10 beans into the cup. Guess how many will land on each side. Say why.
flow.context: This is the first step of Spill the Beans. You count 10 beans into a cup and guess how they will land on a paper with a line down the middle.

ask.q: Why did you guess that?
good: It will change every time, because beans fall anywhere.
More on this side, because I pour from here.

flow.parent: Accept any guess that comes with a reason. Do not say yet that the two sides will make 10.

flow.do: 1. Your child shakes the tumbler and spills the beans from a hand's height. 2. Push any bean on the line to the nearer side. 3. Your child counts the left side, then the right side. 4. Write both numbers. 5. Push all the beans together and count them. Write that number too. 6. Do this six times.
flow.say: Count the left side. Now the right side. Now push them all together. How many are there altogether?
flow.kid: Spill the beans. Count the left side. Count the right side. Then count them all.
flow.context: This is step 2 of Spill the Beans. You spill 10 beans six times onto a paper with a line, and write how many land on each side.

ask.q: The two sides were different this time. Did the number altogether change?

flow.parent: If the count altogether is not 10, a bean has rolled away. Find it before you go on. After three spills, ask your child to say the total before counting.

chart.title: Draw this table and fill it in

flow.do: 1. Look at the spill table together. 2. Ask whether any spill came up twice. 3. If you have both 3 and 7 and 7 and 3, or a pair like that, point to them. 4. Ask how many different ways there could be. Write the guess.
flow.say: Look at our spills. Are any two the same? How many different ways do you think 10 beans can land? Why?
flow.kid: Look at your table. Did any spill come twice? Guess how many ways there are.
flow.context: This is step 3 of Spill the Beans. You look at your table of spills and guess how many different ways 10 beans can be split in two.

ask.q: Is 3 on the left and 7 on the right the same as 7 on the left and 3 on the right?
good: Yes, it is still a 3 and a 7.

flow.parent: Both answers to the question are sensible. Do not settle it yet. Six spills never show every way, so your child cannot know the number of ways from the table alone.

flow.do: 1. Put all 10 beans on the left of the line. 2. Write '10 and 0' in a new table. 3. Your child slides one bean across the line. 4. Before counting, ask what the two numbers are now. Then count and write them. 5. Go on, one bean at a time, until all 10 are on the right.
flow.say: All 10 are on the left. I slide one across. What are the two numbers now? Tell me before you count.
flow.kid: Put all 10 beans on the left. Slide one across. Write the two numbers. Do it again.
flow.context: This is step 4 of Spill the Beans. You start with all 10 beans on the left of the line and slide one bean across at a time, writing each pair of numbers.

ask.q: How did you know the numbers before you counted?
good: The left lost one and the right got one.
It goes down here and up there.

flow.parent: After three or four moves, most children stop counting and say the next pair straight away. That is the pattern showing itself. Let your child say it in their own words.

flow.do: 1. Look at the new table. 2. Ask what happens to the left number as you go down. Ask about the right number. 3. Count the rows together. 4. Ask whether any way could be missing.
flow.say: Look down the left side. What do the numbers do? What do the numbers on the right do? Could we have missed a way?
flow.kid: Read down the left numbers. Read down the right numbers. What do you notice?
flow.context: This is step 5 of Spill the Beans. You look for a pattern in your table of all the ways to split 10 beans.

ask.q: How many rows are there? Could there be another way that is not in the table?
good: No, there is no number between 6 and 5.

flow.parent: There are 11 rows, from 10 and 0 to 0 and 10. If your child treats 3 and 7 and 7 and 3 as one way, there are 6 pairs. Both counts are right. They count different things.

check.q: The left side has 6 beans and the right has 4. One bean slides from left to right. What are the sides now?
check.why: 5 and 5. The left side loses one bean and the right side gains the same bean, so the whole stays 10. Picking 5 and 4 means the bean was taken off the left but not added to the right.

flow.do: 1. Ask your child what they think now, what they saw, and why it is so. 2. Write their words under the tables.
flow.say: What did we find out about 10 beans in two groups? What did you see? Why is it always so?
flow.kid: What did you find out about the two sides? Say what you saw. Say why.
flow.context: This is the last step of Spill the Beans. You say what you found out about splitting 10 beans into two groups.

ask.q: What do you think? What did you see? Why?
good: Because no bean went away. They only changed sides.

check.q: 10 beans are spilled. 8 land on the left side of the line. How many are on the right side?
check.why: 2. The two sides must make 10, and 8 and 2 make 10. Picking 18 means 8 and 10 were added. But 10 is the whole, not a part.

activities.title: Mirror Doubles: see a number twice
activities.context: In this activity you put beans in front of a mirror and count the beans and their mirror picture together. The point is to find the doubles from 1 and 1 up to 5 and 5.
activities.problem: A mirror shows every bean a second time. So how many do you see when you put down 1 bean, 2 beans, 3 beans?

materials.item: a small mirror that can stand up, leaning on a book
dried beans
paper and a pencil

activities.safety: A grown-up sets up and holds the mirror. Keep beans, coins and buttons away from babies and toddlers, who could choke on them.

schedule.what: Put 1 to 5 beans in front of a mirror, guess and count what you see, then show the doubles on your fingers.

activities.record: Draw a table with three columns: beans, beans in the mirror, altogether. Fill in a row for 1, 2, 3, 4 and 5 beans.

setup.art: A small rectangular mirror leaning upright against a thick book on a table, with a sheet of paper lying in front of it.
setup.caption: 1. A grown-up stands the mirror up against a book.

setup.art: Three beans in a row on the paper close to the mirror, and their three reflections in the glass.
setup.caption: 2. Put beans in front of the mirror. Count them and their picture together.

setup.art: A child holding up three fingers on each hand, palms facing each other like a mirror.
setup.caption: 3. Show the same number on both hands. That is a double.

flow.do: 1. Stand the mirror upright against a book. 2. Your child puts 1 bean in front of the mirror. 3. Ask how many beans they can see, counting the one in the mirror. 4. Before putting down 2 beans, ask for a guess.
flow.say: One bean, and one in the mirror. How many can you see? What will you see if you put down 2 beans? Why?
flow.kid: Put 1 bean by the mirror. Count the bean and the picture in the mirror. Now guess for 2 beans.
flow.context: This is the first step of Mirror Doubles. You put beans in front of a mirror and count the beans and their mirror picture together.

ask.q: Why did you guess that?
good: The mirror shows each bean again.

flow.do: 1. Your child puts down 2 beans, then 3, 4 and 5. 2. Each time, ask for a guess first. 3. Then count the beans and their mirror pictures together. 4. Write each row in the table.
flow.say: Now 3 beans. Guess first. How many will you see altogether? Count and check.
flow.kid: Put down 3 beans. Guess how many you will see. Count. Then try 4 and 5.
flow.context: This is step 2 of Mirror Doubles. You put 2, 3, 4 and 5 beans in front of a mirror, and guess before you count the beans and their mirror pictures.

ask.q: Read the last column of your table. Where have you heard these numbers before?

flow.parent: The last column reads 2, 4, 6, 8, 10. Each new bean comes with a mirror partner, so the total goes up by two.

flow.do: 1. Put the mirror away. 2. Your child holds up the same number of fingers on each hand. 3. Call out 'double 2', 'double 5', 'double 3', and so on. 4. Your child shows it on two hands and says the answer.
flow.say: Now your hands are the mirror. Show me double 3. How many fingers is that?
flow.kid: Hold up 3 fingers on each hand. That is double 3. Count them all.
flow.context: This is the last step of Mirror Doubles. You show doubles with the same number of fingers on each hand.

ask.q: What is double 5 on your hands? What else do you call that number?

check.why: 8. Double 4 means 4 and 4 more, which is 8. Picking 6 means 2 was added and not another 4. Picking 44 means the 4 was written twice, not added.

activities.title: Hide and Tell: how many are under the cup?
activities.context: In this activity one person hides some of 10 beans under a cup, and the other says how many are hidden without looking. The point is to know the missing part of 10 from the part you can see.
activities.problem: You know there are 10 beans. You can see some of them. How can you tell how many are hidden?

materials.item: dried beans
a steel tumbler or cup that you cannot see through
paper and a pencil, to draw a ten-frame

activities.safety: Keep beans, coins and buttons away from babies and toddlers, who could choke on them.

schedule.what: Play six rounds of hiding beans under a cup, then use a ten-frame to see the missing part.

activities.record: Draw one round: the beans you could see, the cup, and the number you said was hiding.

setup.art: Ten beans in a row on a table with an upturned steel tumbler beside them.
setup.caption: 1. Count 10 beans together. Everyone agrees there are 10.

setup.art: A child with hands over her eyes while a grown-up slides some beans under the tumbler.
setup.caption: 2. One player shuts their eyes. The other hides some beans under the cup.

setup.art: Six beans placed on a hand-drawn ten-frame with four empty spaces, next to the tumbler.
setup.caption: 3. Put the beans you can see on a ten-frame. The empty spaces tell you how many are hiding.

flow.do: 1. Count 10 beans together. 2. Your child shuts their eyes. 3. Hide 4 beans under the cup. Leave 6 showing. 4. Ask how many are hiding, and how they know. 5. Lift the cup to check.
flow.say: There were 10. Open your eyes. How many are hiding under the cup? How do you know?
flow.kid: There are 10 beans. Shut your eyes. Now look. How many are hiding?
flow.context: This is the first step of Hide and Tell. Some of 10 beans are hidden under a cup, and you say how many without looking.

ask.q: How did you work it out?
good: I counted on from 6 to 10 on my fingers.
I remembered it from the spills.

flow.parent: Any way of working it out is fine at first, also counting on fingers. Wait for the answer. Then lift the cup, so the beans show whether it was right.

chart.title: 10 beans in all. Some are under the cup.

flow.do: 1. Play five more rounds. Hide a different number each time. 2. Then swap: your child hides the beans and you say how many. 3. Say a wrong number once or twice, so that your child can catch it.
flow.say: Your turn to hide them. I will say how many are under the cup. Check me.
flow.kid: Now you hide some beans. Your grown-up says how many. Lift the cup and check.
flow.context: This is step 2 of Hide and Tell. You take turns to hide some of 10 beans under a cup and to say how many are hidden.

ask.q: I said 5 were hiding, but you can see 7. How did you know I was wrong?

flow.parent: Hide 0 beans once, and all 10 once. Both are bonds of 10.

check.q: There are 10 beans. You can see 8. How many are under the cup?
check.why: 2 are under the cup, because 8 and 2 make 10. Picking 18 means 8 and 10 were added. But 10 is all the beans, so the hidden part must be smaller than 10.

flow.do: 1. Draw a ten-frame: a box with two rows of five spaces. 2. Hide some beans again. 3. Your child puts the beans they can see on the ten-frame, top row first. 4. Ask how many spaces are empty. 5. Lift the cup and put the hidden beans in the empty spaces.
flow.say: Put the beans you can see in the box. How many spaces are empty? So how many are hiding?
flow.kid: Put the beans you see on the ten-frame. Count the empty spaces. That many are hiding.
flow.context: This is the last step of Hide and Tell. You put the beans you can see on a ten-frame, a box with two rows of five spaces, and read the hidden number from the empty spaces.

ask.q: Do the hidden beans fit the empty spaces exactly? Why?
good: Because the box holds 10 and there are 10 beans.

flow.parent: Your child's fingers work in the same way: hold up as many fingers as there are beans showing. The folded fingers are the hidden beans.

chart.title: The ten-frame after you put 6 beans on it

activities.title: Maths in the market: pay ten rupees
activities.context: In this activity you make ten rupees from coins in different ways, and then pay for something real with them. The point is to use the bonds of 10 the way shopkeepers and buyers do every day.
activities.problem: Many small things in a shop cost ₹10. How many different ways can you pay ₹10 with coins?

materials.item: ₹1 coins
₹2 coins
₹5 coins
paper and a pencil
if you have no coins: paper circles with 1, 2 and 5 written on them

activities.safety: Coins are a choking risk for babies and toddlers. Wash hands after handling coins.

schedule.what: Sort the coins, make ₹10 in different ways, play shop, and then pay ₹10 in a real shop.

activities.record: Draw each way you found to make ₹10, as a row of coins. Circle the way that uses the fewest coins.

setup.art: Three small heaps of Indian coins on a table: five one-rupee coins, three two-rupee coins and two five-rupee coins.
setup.caption: 1. Sort the coins: ₹1, ₹2 and ₹5.

setup.art: A row of coins on paper: one five-rupee coin, two two-rupee coins and one one-rupee coin, with '10' written at the end.
setup.caption: 2. Lay out coins that make ₹10. Find another way.

setup.art: A girl at a small shop counter putting coins into a shopkeeper's hand, a packet of biscuits on the counter.
setup.caption: 3. Pay ₹10 for something real with your coins.

flow.do: 1. Tip the coins onto the table. 2. Your child sorts them into ₹1, ₹2 and ₹5 heaps. 3. Read the number on each kind of coin together. 4. Show that one ₹5 coin is worth the same as five ₹1 coins by laying them side by side.
flow.say: Find the number on each coin. This one says 5. It is worth the same as five of these ₹1 coins.
flow.kid: Sort the coins into heaps. Find the number on each coin.
flow.context: This is the first step of Maths in the Market. You sort ₹1, ₹2 and ₹5 coins before you use them to make ten rupees.
flow.parent: A ₹5 coin is one thing worth five. This is a new idea for many six-year-olds. Lay five ₹1 coins under the ₹5 coin to show it.

flow.do: 1. Ask your child to lay out coins that make exactly ₹10. 2. Count the rupees together. 3. Draw that way on paper. 4. Ask for a different way. Find at least three ways.
flow.say: Make ten rupees with these coins. Now make ten rupees in a different way.
flow.kid: Lay out coins that make ₹10. Draw them. Then find another way.
flow.context: This is step 2 of Maths in the Market. You find different ways to make ten rupees from ₹1, ₹2 and ₹5 coins.

ask.q: Which way uses the fewest coins? What do we call 5 and 5?

flow.parent: Some ways with these coins: 5 and 5. 5, 2, 2 and 1. 5, 2, 1, 1 and 1. 5 and five 1s. 2, 2, 2 and four 1s. To count a row, start with the biggest coin and count on.

flow.do: 1. Play shop. A small thing on the table costs ₹10. 2. Give your child a ₹5 coin and a ₹2 coin. 3. Ask how much they have, and how much more they need. 4. Play again with other coins.
flow.say: This costs ten rupees. You have these coins. How much do you have? How much more do you need?
flow.kid: The price is ₹10. Count your coins. How many more rupees do you need?
flow.context: This is step 3 of Maths in the Market. You play shop: something costs ten rupees, and you work out how much more money you need.

ask.q: You have ₹7. How much more makes ₹10?

check.q: A packet costs ₹10. You have ₹6. How many more rupees do you need?
check.why: ₹4, because 6 and 4 make 10. Picking ₹16 means the two numbers were added. The question asks for the missing part of 10.

flow.do: 1. The next time you go to a shop, take the coins. 2. Choose something that costs ₹10. 3. Your child counts out the ₹10 and pays. 4. On the way home, ask which coins they used.
flow.say: You are paying today. Count out ten rupees for the shopkeeper.
flow.kid: At the shop, count out ₹10 in coins. Pay with them yourself.
flow.context: This is the last step of Maths in the Market. You pay ten rupees in a real shop with coins you have counted yourself.
flow.parent: This step can wait for your next trip to a shop. Many small packets of biscuits and many pencils cost ₹10. If the shop is busy, count the coins out before you reach the counter.

activities.title: Maths in cricket: how many wickets are left?
activities.context: In this activity you keep track of wickets the way a cricket scorer does. In a full match a team stops batting when 10 wickets have fallen. The point is to say the wickets left from the wickets fallen, using the bonds of 10.
activities.problem: A cricket team has 10 wickets to lose. If you know how many have fallen, you know how many are left.

materials.item: bottle caps, clothes pegs or beans, to stand for wickets
paper and a pencil

schedule.what: Stand up 10 pretend wickets, knock some down, and say how many are left. Then read the wickets from a real scoreboard.

activities.record: Write a scoreboard line for your pretend match, such as '4 wickets down, 6 left'.

setup.art: Ten clothes pegs standing in two rows of five on a floor, like a ten-frame.
setup.caption: 1. Stand up 10 pegs in two rows of five. These are the team's 10 wickets.

setup.art: Three of the ten pegs lying flat and seven still standing, with a child pointing at the standing ones.
setup.caption: 2. 'Three wickets down!' Lay 3 pegs flat. How many are left?

setup.art: A television screen showing a cricket score written as 86-4, with a child holding up four fingers.
setup.caption: 3. On a real scoreboard, find the wickets fallen. Say the wickets left.

flow.do: 1. Stand 10 pegs or caps in two rows of five. 2. Explain that a team's turn to bat ends when 10 wickets have fallen. 3. Ask how many wickets the team has left before anyone is out.
flow.say: A team has 10 wickets. Each time a batter is out, one wicket falls. Nobody is out yet. How many wickets are left?
flow.kid: Stand up 10 pegs in two rows of five. These are your team's 10 wickets.
flow.context: This is the first step of Maths in Cricket. You set up 10 pegs to stand for the 10 wickets a cricket team can lose.
flow.parent: A cricket team has 11 players, but the last batter cannot bat alone. So the innings ends at 10 wickets.

flow.do: 1. Call out 'Two wickets down!' 2. Your child lays 2 pegs flat and says how many are left. 3. Call out more wickets, one or two at a time, until all 10 are down. 4. Each time, your child says the wickets fallen and the wickets left.
flow.say: Another wicket! How many have fallen now? How many are left?
flow.kid: Lay a peg flat for each wicket that falls. Say how many are left.
flow.context: This is step 2 of Maths in Cricket. Ten pegs stand for a team's 10 wickets, and you say how many are left each time one falls.

ask.q: 7 wickets have fallen. How many are left?

check.q: In a cricket match, 6 of a team's 10 wickets have fallen. How many wickets are left?
check.why: 4 wickets are left, because 6 and 4 make 10. Picking 16 means 6 and 10 were added. But 10 is all the wickets there are.

flow.do: 1. Find a real cricket score, on television, in a newspaper or on a phone. 2. Show your child the number of wickets. A score such as 86-4 means 86 runs and 4 wickets fallen. 3. Your child says how many wickets are left.
flow.say: This score says 4 wickets have fallen. How many wickets does the team still have?
flow.kid: Find the wickets on a real scoreboard. Say how many are left.
flow.context: This is the last step of Maths in Cricket. You read the wickets fallen from a real cricket score and say how many of the 10 are left.
flow.parent: Commentators say 'six wickets in hand' for six wickets left. If no match is on, look up the score of any past match.

games.title: Ten Pairs
games.players: 1 to 4 players: alone, with a parent or with friends
games.context: This is a memory game played with number cards from 0 to 10. You turn over two cards and keep them if they make 10. It builds quick recall of the bonds of 10.

printables.title: 22 number cards: two each of 0 to 10

rules: Mix the 22 cards. Lay them face down in rows.
On your turn, turn over two cards. Say the two numbers aloud.
If the two numbers make 10, say the bond, such as '6 and 4 make 10'. Keep the pair and take another turn.
If they do not make 10, turn them face down again in the same places. The next player goes.
The game ends when every card has been taken. The player with the most pairs wins.
Playing alone: count how many turns you need to clear the table. Play again and try to need fewer.
No printer? Write the numbers on slips of paper. Or use playing cards from Ace to 9 in two suits, with the Ace as 1.

setup.art: Twenty-two small paper cards face down on a floor in four neat rows.
setup.caption: 1. Mix the cards. Lay them face down.

setup.art: A child's hand turning over two cards showing 7 and 3, with a speech bubble '7 and 3 make 10'.
setup.caption: 2. Turn over two cards. If they make 10, keep them.

setup.art: Two cards showing 6 and 5 being turned face down again in their places.
setup.caption: 3. If they do not make 10, turn them back.

flow.do: 1. Cut out the 22 cards, or write 0 to 10 twice on slips of paper. 2. Lay them face up in order first. 3. Ask your child to point to the two cards at the ends, and say whether they make 10.
flow.say: Here are the cards from 0 to 10. Which card goes with 0 to make 10? Which goes with 1?
flow.kid: Lay the cards in order from 0 to 10. Find the partner of 0.
flow.context: This is the first step of Ten Pairs, a memory game with number cards from 0 to 10. Here you look at the cards and find which ones go together to make 10.

flow.do: 1. Play one round with all the cards face up. 2. Take turns to pick up two cards that make 10 and say the bond. 3. Go on until no cards are left.
flow.say: The cards are face up this time. Pick any two that make 10 and tell me the bond.
flow.kid: Pick up two cards that make 10. Say the bond aloud.
flow.context: This is step 2 of Ten Pairs, a game with number cards from 0 to 10. Here you practise with the cards face up, picking pairs that make 10.
flow.parent: The two 5s go together. Every other card needs a different number as its partner.

check.q: In Ten Pairs you turn over a 4. Which card do you need to make 10?
check.why: You need a 6, because 4 and 6 make 10. Picking 4 would make a double, 4 and 4, which is 8.

flow.do: 1. Mix the cards and lay them face down in rows. 2. Play the memory game by the rules. 3. Each time a player turns over the first card, ask which card they are hoping for.
flow.say: You turned over an 8. Which number are you hoping for? Can you remember where it is?
flow.kid: Turn over two cards. If they make 10, keep them and go again.
flow.context: This is step 3 of Ten Pairs, a memory game with number cards from 0 to 10. Here you play with the cards face down.

ask.q: You turned over a 3. Which number are you hoping for?

flow.do: 1. When all the cards are taken, each player counts their pairs. 2. Lay all the pairs in order, from 0 and 10 to 5 and 5. 3. Read them aloud together.
flow.say: Count your pairs. Now let us lay all the pairs in order and read them.
flow.kid: Count your pairs. Lay them in order. Read every bond aloud.
flow.context: This is the last step of Ten Pairs, a memory game with number cards from 0 to 10. Here you count your pairs and read all the bonds of 10 in order.

games.title: Double It
games.players: 1 to 4 players: alone, with a parent or with friends
games.context: This is a dice game. You roll one dice, double the number, and cover the answer on your strip. It builds quick recall of the doubles.

printables.title: A doubles strip: 6 boxes in a row (one strip for each player)

rules: Each player has a doubles strip and 6 beans. To make a strip by hand, draw 6 boxes in a row and write 2, 4, 6, 8, 10, 12 in them.
On your turn, roll the dice. Say the double aloud, such as 'double 3 is 6'.
Put a bean on that number on your strip. If it is already covered, do nothing.
If another player thinks your double is wrong, they say 'check'. Show the double on your fingers or with beans. If you were wrong, you do not cover a number this turn.
The first player to cover all 6 numbers wins.
Playing alone: count how many rolls you need to cover your strip. Play again and try to need fewer.

setup.art: A paper strip of six boxes marked 2, 4, 6, 8, 10 and 12, with six beans and a dice beside it.
setup.caption: 1. Each player takes a strip and 6 beans.

setup.art: A dice showing 3 and a child holding up three fingers on each hand.
setup.caption: 2. Roll the dice. Say the double.

setup.art: A hand placing a bean on the box marked 6 on the strip.
setup.caption: 3. Cover the answer on your strip.

flow.do: 1. Give each player a strip and 6 beans. 2. Read the numbers on the strip together. 3. Ask which dice number each box belongs to.
flow.say: Each box is the double of a dice number. Which dice number do you need to cover the 8?
flow.kid: Take a strip and 6 beans. Read the numbers on your strip.
flow.context: This is the first step of Double It, a dice game for learning doubles. Here you look at the strip of answers: 2, 4, 6, 8, 10 and 12.

flow.do: 1. Take one practice turn each. 2. Roll, say the double, and cover it. 3. For a 6, show how to work it out: double 5 is 10, and two more is 12.
flow.say: I rolled 6. Double 5 is 10, and one more on each side makes 12. Now you roll.
flow.kid: Roll the dice. Say the double. Cover that number with a bean.
flow.context: This is step 2 of Double It, a dice game for learning doubles. Here you practise one turn each.
flow.parent: Double 6 is past the doubles of this lesson. It is in the game because a dice has a 6. Let your child use beans for it.

check.q: In Double It you roll a 3. Which number do you cover?
check.why: You cover 6, because double 3 is 3 and 3, which is 6. Picking 5 means 2 was added and not another 3.

flow.do: 1. Play until someone covers all 6 numbers. 2. Say 'check' once or twice, so that players show a double on their fingers. 3. Near the end, ask which dice number a player is hoping for.
flow.say: You still need the 10. Which dice number are you hoping for?
flow.kid: Play the game. Say each double aloud. Cover all 6 numbers to win.
flow.context: This is step 3 of Double It, a dice game for learning doubles. Here you play until one strip is full.

ask.q: You need to cover the 8. Which dice number do you want?

flow.do: 1. When the game ends, read the strip aloud together. 2. Ask what the numbers have in common.
flow.say: Read the numbers on the strip. What kind of counting is this?
flow.kid: Read the numbers on your strip aloud. What do you notice?
flow.context: This is the last step of Double It, a dice game for learning doubles. Here you read the answers aloud: 2, 4, 6, 8, 10, 12.

ask.q: Why is there no 7 on the strip?
good: 7 cannot be two parts the same.
It is not in counting in twos.

projects.title: My Book of Ten: five days, five tens
projects.context: In this five-day project you find 10 of something at home each day, split it into two groups, and draw it. On the last day you put the pages together into a small book of bonds of 10.
projects.problem: Bonds of 10 stick in your memory when you meet them in real things, a little every day.

materials.item: half sheets of paper, one for each day, and one for the cover
a pencil and crayons
things to sort at home: spoons, clothes pegs, chappals, vegetables, bangles
thread or a stapler, to join the pages

projects.safety: A grown-up uses the stapler or the needle on day 5.

schedule.what: Take 10 spoons. Split them into two groups, such as big and small. Draw them and write the bond.
Take 10 clothes pegs. Clip some on one edge of a plate and the rest on the other. Draw and write the bond.
Take 10 vegetables or fruits. Split them a new way. Draw and write the bond.
Choose your own 10 things. Split them so that you get a bond you have not drawn yet.
Put the pages in order. Find which bonds of 10 are missing. Make a cover and join the book.

projects.record: Each page shows the 10 things in two groups and one line of writing: '__ and __ make 10'.

setup.art: Ten steel spoons on a table sorted into a group of six big spoons and a group of four small spoons.
setup.caption: 1. Find 10 of something. Split it into two groups.

setup.art: A half sheet of paper with a child's drawing of six big spoons and four small spoons and the words '6 and 4 make 10'.
setup.caption: 2. Draw the two groups. Write the bond.

setup.art: Five drawn pages and a cover laid in a row, being stitched together along one edge with thread.
setup.caption: 3. On day 5, put the pages in order and join them into a book.

flow.do: 1. Your child counts out 10 spoons. 2. They split the spoons into two groups in any way they choose. 3. They draw the two groups on a half sheet. 4. Write the bond together under the drawing.
flow.say: Count out 10 spoons. Put them in two groups, any way you like. What is your bond today?
flow.kid: Count 10 spoons. Make two groups. Draw them. Write the bond.
flow.context: This is day 1 of My Book of Ten, a five-day project. Each day you split 10 things into two groups and draw the bond.

flow.do: 1. On days 2, 3 and 4, use a new kind of thing each day. 2. Before your child splits the things, look at the pages so far. 3. Ask for a bond that is not in the book yet. 4. Your child draws it and writes the bond.
flow.say: Which bonds do we already have in the book? Can you make a new one today?
flow.kid: Look at your pages. Make a bond you do not have yet. Draw it.
flow.context: These are days 2 to 4 of My Book of Ten, a five-day project. Each day you split 10 new things into two groups and draw a bond you have not drawn yet.

ask.q: You have 6 and 4. Is 4 and 6 a new bond, or the same one?

flow.parent: Either answer about turn-arounds is fine, as long as your child can say why.
flow.wait: Do this on each of the next three days.

flow.do: 1. On day 5, lay the pages in order, starting with the page whose first number is biggest. 2. Ask which bonds of 10 are missing. 3. Your child makes a cover. 4. Join the pages with a stapler or thread.
flow.say: Put your pages in order. There are 6 different pairs that make 10. Which ones are not in your book yet?
flow.kid: Put your pages in order. Which bonds are missing? Make a cover.
flow.context: This is day 5 of My Book of Ten, a five-day project. Today you put your pages of bonds of 10 in order and find which bonds are missing.

ask.q: How do you know which bonds are missing?
good: I said them in order: 10 and 0, 9 and 1, 8 and 2.
I looked for each number from 0 to 5.

flow.parent: The 6 pairs are 10 and 0, 9 and 1, 8 and 2, 7 and 3, 6 and 4, 5 and 5. Four pages cannot show them all. Your child can add pages later.

challenges.title: Stretch: ten laddus on three plates
challenges.context: This is a puzzle that goes past Class 1. You share 10 beans, standing for laddus, among three plates in every way you can. Then you invent a way to be sure you have not missed any.
challenges.problem: Ten laddus must go on three plates. No plate may be empty. How many different ways are there? Your way of working must show that none is missing.
constraints: All 10 beans must be used every time.
The plates are all alike. So 5, 3 and 2 is the same way as 2, 3 and 5.
You must be able to explain why you are sure you have every way.
general: Try any split, write it down, and try another.
Start from a way you have, and move one bean from one plate to another.
Write each way with the biggest number first, so that you can spot a way you already have.
creative: Go in order. Put as many as you can on the first plate: 8, 1 and 1. Then make the first plate 7, then 6, and so on.
For each number on the first plate, list every way to share the rest between the other two plates.

items.p: Count the beans. ____ more make 10.
items.why: There are 8 beans. 8 and 2 make 10. You can count on from 8: 9, 10. That is 2 more.

items.p: 6 and which number make 10?
items.why: 6 and 4 make 10. On a ten-frame, 6 beans leave 4 empty spaces.

items.p: 5 and 5 make 10.
items.why: True. One hand has 5 fingers and the other has 5. Together they are 10.

items.p: 9 and ____ make 10.
items.why: 9 and 1 make 10. Ten is the next number after 9, so only 1 more is needed.

items.p: Match each number to its partner that makes 10.
items.why: 1 and 9, 2 and 8, 3 and 7, and 4 and 6 each make 10. As one part goes up by one, the other part goes down by one.

items.p: What is double 2?
items.why: Double 2 is 2 and 2 more, which is 4. Picking 22 means the 2 was written twice, not added.

items.p: 3 and 3 make ____.
items.why: 3 and 3 make 6. This is double 3. Hold up 3 fingers on each hand and count them.

items.p: 7 and 2 make 10.
items.why: False. 7 and 2 make 9. The partner of 7 is 3, because 7 and 3 make 10.

items.p: A box has 10 spaces for laddus. 7 spaces are full. How many more laddus fit?
items.why: 3 more fit. 7 and 3 make 10. You can count the empty spaces in the picture.

items.p: Put these doubles in order, smallest answer first.
items.why: The answers are 2, 4, 6, 8 and 10. A double of a bigger number gives a bigger answer.

items.p: Draw double 3 with dots: 3 dots in a row, and 3 more under them. Write how many dots.
items.a: Two rows of 3 dots, one under the other, and the number 6.
items.why: Double 3 is 3 and 3, which is 6. Each dot in the top row has a partner under it.

items.p: Draw a ten-frame. Put 4 red dots in it. Fill the rest with blue dots. Write how many blue dots.
items.a: A box with two rows of five, 4 red dots and 6 blue dots, and the number 6.
items.why: A ten-frame holds 10. 4 and 6 make 10, so 6 spaces are left for blue.

items.p: Say your answer aloud. A grown-up writes it. In Spill the Beans, why did the two sides always make 10?
items.a: Because we used the same 10 beans every time. No bean was added or taken away. They only landed on different sides.
items.why: A strong answer says that the beans only changed sides, so the whole stayed 10.

items.p: ____ and 2 make 10.
items.why: 8 and 2 make 10. It is the turn-around of 2 and 8.
4 and 6 make 10. On a ten-frame, 4 beans leave 6 empty spaces.

items.p: Which pair does NOT make 10?
items.why: 7 and 4 make 11, which is one too many. The partner of 7 is 3.

items.p: 3 and 7 make the same number as 7 and 3.
items.why: True. They are the same two parts in a different order. Both make 10.

items.p: Sort each pair: does it make 10, or not?
items.why: 8 and 2, 0 and 10, and 7 and 3 make 10. 5 and 4 make 9. 6 and 3 make 9. 9 and 2 make 11.

items.p: There are 10 beans. You can see 4. How many are under the cup?
items.why: 6 are under the cup, because 4 and 6 make 10. Picking 14 means 4 and 10 were added. But 10 is all the beans.

items.p: Double 5 is ____.
items.why: Double 5 is 5 and 5, which is 10. It is both a double and a bond of 10.

items.p: Which of these is a double?
items.why: 4 and 4 is a double, because both parts are the same. 4 and 6 is a bond of 10, but it is not a double.

items.p: A pencil costs ₹10. You have a ₹5 coin and a ₹2 coin. How many more rupees do you need?
items.why: You have 5 and 2, which is ₹7. 7 and 3 make 10, so you need ₹3 more. Picking ₹7 gives what you have, not what you need.

items.p: In a cricket match, 6 of a team's 10 wickets have fallen. ____ wickets are left.
items.why: 6 and 4 make 10. So 4 wickets are left.

items.p: Draw your two hands with 7 fingers up. Write how many fingers are folded down.
items.a: Two hands with 7 fingers up and 3 folded down, and the number 3.
items.why: You have 10 fingers. 7 and 3 make 10, so 3 are folded down.

items.p: A sweet costs ₹10 and you have ₹8. How much more do you need? Say how you know.
items.why: A strong answer gives the bond: 8 and 2 make 10. Counting on from 8 to 10 is also a good way.

items.p: Ten beans are on the left. One bean moves to the right each time. Put the bonds in the order they come.
items.why: Each move takes one from the left and gives one to the right. The first number goes down by one each time.

items.p: How many ways are there to split 10 beans between a left side and a right side?

views.says: Eleven. 3 on the left and 7 on the right is not the same as 7 on the left and 3 on the right.
Six. 3 and 7 is the same pair as 7 and 3.

items.ask: Who do you agree with? Why? Then say one thing the other person has right.
items.a: A strong answer picks a side with a reason, then says what the other count is counting. There are 11 ways if the sides matter and 6 pairs if they do not.
items.why: Both counts are correct. They count different things. Before counting ways, you have to choose what counts as a different way.

items.p: This goes past Class 1. Double 6 is ____.
items.why: Double 5 is 10. Double 6 has one more on each side, so it is 10 and 2 more, which is 12.

items.p: 4 and 4 and 2 make ____.
items.why: Double 4 is 8. Then 8 and 2 make 10.

items.p: This goes past Class 1. What is 8 + 5? Fill the ten first.
items.why: 8 and 2 make 10. That uses 2 of the 5, and 3 are left. 10 and 3 is 13.

items.p: Double a number is 8. What is the number?
items.why: 4, because 4 and 4 make 8. Picking 16 means 8 was doubled. The question asks which number was doubled to get 8.

items.p: If 6 and 4 make 10, then 10 take away 6 leaves 4.
items.why: True. 10 is made of the parts 6 and 4. Take one part away and the other part is left.

items.p: Which number is its own partner to make 10?
items.why: 5, because 5 and 5 make 10. It is the only bond of 10 that is also a double.

items.p: 10 and ____ make 10.
items.why: 10 and 0 make 10. Adding zero changes nothing.

items.p: The answer to a double is always a number you say when you count in twos.
items.why: True. A double is made of pairs, one from each part. So the answers are 2, 4, 6, 8, 10 and so on.

items.p: Match each double to its answer.
items.why: Double 2 is 2 and 2. Double 3 is 3 and 3. Double 4 is 4 and 4. Double 5 is 5 and 5.

items.p: Sort each pair: less than 10, exactly 10, or more than 10?
items.why: Compare each pair with a bond you know. 5 and 5 make 10, so 4 and 5 is one less and 6 and 5 is one more. 7 and 3 make 10, so 2 and 7 is one less and 8 and 3 is one more.

items.p: 7 beans are on the left and 3 on the right. One bean moves to the right. Now the right has ____.
items.why: The right side gains one bean: 3 and 1 more is 4. The left side now has 6. 6 and 4 still make 10.

items.p: Draw 8 + 5 with dots. Fill a ten-frame first. Draw the dots left over beside it. Write the answer.
items.a: A full ten-frame, 3 dots beside it, and the number 13.
items.why: 8 and 2 make 10. That uses 2 of the 5 dots. 3 are left over, and 10 and 3 is 13.

items.p: 10 laddus go on 3 plates. No plate is empty. Write three different ways.
items.why: Each way must use all 10 laddus. Check by adding the three numbers.

items.p: Is ten a special number?

views.says: Yes. We have ten fingers, and we write all our numbers in tens.
No. Eight beans or twelve beans can be split into two parts just as well.

items.ask: Who do you agree with? Why? Then say one thing the other person has right.
items.a: A strong answer picks a side with a reason from the unit. For example: making ten helps with every bigger sum, or people in some places counted in eights and twenties.
items.why: Both have a point. Ten is special to people, because of our fingers and our way of writing numbers. The beans themselves do not treat ten differently.

quiz.why: 6 and 4 make 10. 6 and 3 make 9, and 6 and 5 make 11.
2 and 8 make 10. It is the turn-around of 8 and 2.

quiz.p: There are 10 beans. You can see 7. How many are under the cup?
quiz.why: 3 are under the cup, because 7 and 3 make 10. Picking 17 means 7 and 10 were added. But 10 is all the beans.

quiz.p: A boat has 10 seats. 9 seats are taken. ____ seat is free.
quiz.why: 9 and 1 make 10. So 1 seat is free.

quiz.p: 4 and 6 make 10. So 6 and 4 make 10 too.
quiz.why: True. They are the same two parts in the other order. The whole does not change.

quiz.p: 8 beans are on the left and 2 are on the right. The two sides swap places. How many beans are there altogether?
quiz.why: Still 10. Swapping the sides does not add or take away a bean. 2 and 8 make the same 10 as 8 and 2.
Double 4 is 8. Hold up 4 fingers on each hand and count them.
Double 5 is 5 and 5, which is 10. Picking 55 means the 5 was written twice, not added.

quiz.p: A ten-frame has 6 beans on it. How many spaces are empty?
quiz.why: 4 spaces are empty. A ten-frame holds 10, and 6 and 4 make 10.

quiz.p: You hold up 7 fingers. How many fingers are folded down?
quiz.why: 3 are folded down. You have 10 fingers, and 7 and 3 make 10.

quiz.p: Why do most people group things in tens?
quiz.why: The most likely reason is our ten fingers. Beans do not come in tens, and there is no biggest number.

quiz.p: Only the number 10 can be split into two parts.
quiz.why: False. Other numbers can be split too. For example, 8 is 5 and 3, and 6 is 4 and 2.

maths.problem: In a cricket match, 7 of a team's 10 wickets have fallen. How many wickets are left?
maths.explain: A team has 10 wickets. 7 and 3 make 10. So 3 wickets are left.
maths.context: In Maths in Cricket you laid pegs flat for wickets that fell and said how many were left. This is the same question without the pegs.
maths.why_maths: Knowing the bonds of 10 lets you read a scoreboard at a glance, without counting.

maths.problem: A pencil costs ₹10. Kavya has a ₹5 coin and a ₹2 coin. How many more rupees does she need?
maths.explain: Kavya has 5 and 2, which is ₹7. 7 and 3 make 10. So she needs ₹3 more.
maths.context: In Maths in the Market you made ten rupees from coins and played shop. This uses the same idea.
maths.why_maths: A bond of 10 tells a buyer how much more to pay, and tells a shopkeeper how much change to give.

maths.problem: An idli stand has 2 plates. Each plate holds 4 idlis. How many idlis are steamed at one time?
maths.explain: Both plates hold the same number, so this is a double. Double 4 is 4 and 4, which is 8.
maths.context: In Mirror Doubles you saw each bean twice and found the doubles. Two plates with the same number of idlis are a double too.
maths.why_maths: When two groups are the same size, knowing the double is quicker than counting every idli.

maths.problem: Lakshmi wrote the ways to split 10 beans in order, moving one bean at a time. One row got rubbed out. The row above it says 7 and 3. The row below it says 5 and 5. What did the missing row say?
maths.explain: Each row has one fewer on the left and one more on the right. One fewer than 7 is 6. One more than 3 is 4. Check: 6 and 4 make 10.
maths.context: In Spill the Beans you moved one bean across the line at a time and wrote each pair. This uses the pattern you found.
maths.why_maths: A pattern lets you fill in a number you cannot see, and check that no way is missing.

maths.problem: This goes past Class 1. There are 8 beans on a ten-frame. You have 5 more beans to add. How many beans are there altogether?
maths.explain: The ten-frame has 2 empty spaces. Fill them with 2 of the 5 beans. Now the frame is full, which is 10. 3 beans are left over. 10 and 3 is 13.
maths.context: In Hide and Tell you put beans on a ten-frame and read the missing part from the empty spaces. Here you use the empty spaces to add.
maths.why_maths: Filling a ten first turns a hard sum into an easy one. This is why people learn the bonds of 10 by heart.

roots.thread: Ten is one whole. You can break it into 7 and 3, or 6 and 4, or 5 and 5. These are many pairs, but it is the same ten every time. Nothing is lost when you break it, and nothing is added when you join it again. Why ten, and not eight or twelve? People chose ten, most likely because we have ten fingers. The beans did not choose it.

how_we_found_out.context: How did people find out the best way for children to learn sums such as 7 and 3 make 10? This card tells the true story.
how_we_found_out.story: For a long time, schools taught sums by drill. Children said '7 and 3 are 10' again and again until they could answer fast. In 1922 an American scientist, Edward Thorndike, wrote a book called The Psychology of Arithmetic. He said each sum was a 'bond' in the mind, and that practice made the bond strong. Many schools took this to mean that drill was enough. In 1935 William Brownell and C. B. Chazal looked at this with children in Class 3, after weeks of drill. They did something new. They did not only mark the answers and time them. They sat with each child and asked, 'How did you get that?' Two children could give the same right answer, just as fast. One knew the fact. The other was still counting. A clock could not tell them apart. Brownell and Chazal concluded that drill helps only after teaching that makes sense to the child. Teachers still argue about how much practice is needed.
how_we_found_out.who: Edward Thorndike, and later William Brownell and C. B. Chazal
how_we_found_out.wrong_idea: If a child gives the right answer fast after drill, the child has learned the sum. Brownell and Chazal showed in 1935 that this was wrong. When they asked children how they got their answers, some fast children were still counting.

Howard, S. R., Avarguès-Weber, A., Garcia, J. E., Greentree, A. D. and Dyer, A. G. (2019). Numerical cognition in honeybees enables addition and subtraction. Science Advances 5, eaav0961. (14 bees. Blue meant one more, yellow one fewer. Correct in about 60 to 75 percent of choices.)
Thorndike, E. L. (1922). The Psychology of Arithmetic. Macmillan. (The chapter 'The Psychology of Drill in Arithmetic: The Strength of Bonds'.)

Brownell, W. A. and Chazal, C. B. (1935). The effects of premature drill in third-grade arithmetic. Journal of Educational Research 29, 17-28. (Read through later summaries only: they interviewed children about how they got answers, and concluded that drill must be preceded by sound instruction.)
Wynn, K. (1992). Addition and subtraction by human infants. Nature 358, 749-750.
Brahmagupta, Brahmasphutasiddhanta (628 CE), chapter 18: rules for calculating with zero.
Yuki counting in eights, using the spaces between the fingers: reported in several secondary sources. No primary source was read.
Counting on the three joints of each finger with the thumb, to 12 on one hand: described for India and other parts of Asia in general references on finger counting.
The Laws of Cricket: an innings ends when 10 of the 11 batters are out.

playtest: Walked through every flow as a family of two in a flat. Spill the Beans needs 10 beans, a tumbler and a paper with a line. Beans bounce on a bare table, so the paper goes on a towel or in a tray, and the beans are spilled from a hand's height. Six spills never show all 11 ways, which is why step 4 moves one bean at a time. Hide and Tell needs a cup you cannot see through. Mirror Doubles needs a mirror that stands up, held by a grown-up. With no mirror, do only the finger step. The coin activity was checked against the coins listed: five ₹1, three ₹2 and two ₹5 coins make ₹10 in at least five ways. Ten Pairs was played in the head: the 22 cards always pair up fully, and 11 pairs means two players cannot tie. Double It needs about 15 rolls for each player to cover the strip. The three plates puzzle has exactly 8 ways, listed in the parent note. Step minutes add up to each part's minutes. Facts looked up on the web while writing: the 2009 chick study (read in full), the 2019 honeybee study, Thorndike's 1922 book, Brahmagupta's rules for zero, counting in eights by the Yuki, and finger-joint counting. The 1935 study by Brownell and Chazal was read only through later summaries, so the story keeps to what those summaries say. The three videos were confirmed by title and channel only, not watched, so watch each one before showing it.
